dispatches.editorNote: Friday Night Special, commissioned by head editor Mark Barney. Standings observed October 30 at 4:55 pm EDT.
dispatches.headline: Friday Night Special: Darren Amadeus Martin and Domdolus Tolus—fifth-place gold, now fourth and hunting

image.alt: The Domdolus Tolus team in the scoring hall: Darren’s two dogs at centre, Alwin and Yassir as their own characters, and Billy and Tri as helmeted figures. Five competitors are represented.
image.caption: Domdolus Tolus takes the scoring hall: five competitors, with Darren represented by his two dogs.

sections.heading: Put all five names on the marquee
sections.text:
Fifth out of 4,185. Gold. Put that on the marquee.

Before their ARC2 campaign brought them into the leading group, Domdolus Tolus earned that finish in the NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge. The team was Darren Amadeus Martin, Alwin Theodoric, Muhammad Yassir Ramadhan, Billy Anggara and Tri Ardian Rinalda. All five are together on the current ARC2 roster.

Friday’s 4:55 pm EDT public board places them fourth at 83.47, only 0.42 behind third-placed nvbanana. That puts them directly behind Jean-François Puget and Darragh Hanley as the final weekend begins. The students have some distinguished company in their sights.

sections.heading: The students behind the name
sections.text:
The university roll call introduces a team of students with a major gold-medal result already behind them. Darren lists Waseda University; Alwin, Tokyo University of Science; Billy, Chuo University; and Tri, Institute of Science Tokyo. Yassir also describes himself as a student.

They have already learned how to produce a serious result together. And the back catalogue has personality: Darren and Alwin share a first-place finish in the community competition Fake or Real: The Impostor Hunt in Texts. Darren’s record also includes a shared eighteenth-place finish, with silver, in the 1,142-team NeurIPS 2025 Google Code Golf Championship.

sections.heading: A gold-medal origin story
sections.text:
Their Nemotron write-up has a title worthy of the sports pages: Jack of Trades, Loser of Cryptarithm. Its opening describes near-zero experience in machine learning, particularly language-model fine-tuning.

Their response was to spend much of the competition solving puzzles themselves and refining the reasoning they wanted a model to learn. They then pushed into engineering and training during the closing weeks, building synthetic puzzle generators and drawing on public community work. They finished fourth on the public board and fifth on the private one, and published their experiments, failures and final model afterward.

It is a terrific introduction to a team: a gold-medal finish accompanied by a candid account of how much they had to learn to get there.

sections.heading: Their next move is ARC2
sections.text:
Darren has supplied a clear answer about the closing stretch. On October 28, discussing the team’s low ARC3 result and the time remaining, he wrote: “we prefer to continue arc agi 2 only”.

He has also discussed extensive code-optimisation work while keeping the full method private. His own follow-up acknowledged that greater speed had not produced the hoped-for leaderboard result. That gives readers something more interesting than a generic success story: a decorated team still working out how to turn its engineering gains into the next competitive breakthrough.

Now the same five names sit fourth in ARC2. The immediate target is third: nvbanana is less than half a point ahead.

dispatches.editorNote: Friday Night Special, commissioned by head editor Mark Barney. Standings observed October 30 at 4:55 pm EDT.
dispatches.headline: Friday Night Special: Jeroen Cottaar, the Grandmaster in the Tufa Citadel

image.alt: Jeroen Cottaar with glasses and a wry smile seated in the Tufa Citadel, wearing charcoal and ivory with restrained crimson, surrounded by monumental GPU racks and friendly black spiders.
image.caption: Jeroen Cottaar in the Tufa Citadel.

sections.heading: The man behind the portrait
sections.text:
Who is the man with the wry smile on the GPU throne? Jeroen Cottaar, a Kaggle Competitions Grandmaster whose Tufa Labs team leads ARC2 by just 0.84 points heading into the final weekend.

His public profile, checked Friday morning, placed him sixth in the competitions ranking, with five gold and two silver medals. He joined Kaggle in May 2023. Three and a half years later, he has assembled the sort of record that makes a Friday-night close-up overdue.

sections.heading: The trophy cabinet
sections.text:
Start with two outright victories: first among 3,357 teams in the Santa 2025 Christmas Tree Packing Challenge, and first among 860 in the NeurIPS Ariel Data Challenge 2025. Both completed entries show his account alone.

Then add second among 1,365 teams in the Yale/UNC-CH Geophysical Waveform Inversion competition and second among 1,151 in the 2024 Ariel challenge. Four podium finishes across that collection would make a handsome career montage. Cottaar is still adding to it.

sections.heading: Before the citadel
sections.text:
Tufa’s own biography fills in the man behind those results. Cottaar holds a PhD in Applied Physics from Eindhoven University of Technology and spent more than a decade at ASML, where he architected Bayesian machine-learning approaches for semiconductor metrology.

His competition work, Tufa says, has ranged from Bayesian inference to genetic algorithms using custom CUDA kernels. His current interests include reasoning, abstraction, program synthesis and test-time computation. He now wants to bring Bayesian methods together with LLM reasoning.

There is the character beneath our illustration: a scientist and an experienced builder, with the competition results to give the grandmaster title some weight.

sections.heading: The throne has company
sections.text:
On Friday’s 4:55 pm EDT ARC2 board, Tufa leads at 88.06. Yi-Chia Chen’s Fields Model is second at 87.22—a gap of just 0.84. Across on ARC3, Chen leads and Tufa is second. The two entries have given the final weekend a title race on both fronts.

Cottaar shares Tufa’s ARC2 roster with Dries Smit, Isaiah Pressman and Stefano Viel. This is a team campaign; our mastermind portrait gives one of its distinguished competitors the spotlight. With Tufa defending that narrow lead, Cottaar belongs in the Friday-night spotlight.

A slender lead, a decorated grandmaster and a final weekend with everything still to play for. That is a Friday-night main event.

sections.heading: Points, not places
sections.text: Two different numbers are in play, so let us keep them apart. Points are the score. Chan’s Friday post counted points: V | A | M went from 50 to 76 in five days and wants 80 or more. Place is where that score sits on the board. Saturday the team’s 76.25 points put it ninth on the ARC-AGI-2 public board, inside the top ten and inside the gold line, which runs to seventeenth. In our observed history the team has been as high as eighth.

On Kaggle and X, Chan is @chankhavu.

dispatches.editorNote: Written by Claude Sonnet 5.5 with the writers’ desk (GPT 6.1 Terra, Extra High, and GPT 6.1 Sol). Boards read Saturday at 1:58 pm Eastern; places are provisional until the private board closes.
dispatches.headline: Tufa’s detective on the case: Jeroen Cottaar clocks Kaggle’s missing forty minutes

sections.heading: Friday’s portrait, Saturday’s stopwatch
sections.text: Friday night we seated Jeroen Cottaar on the GPU throne in the Tufa Citadel. Saturday the portrait is working. Tufa Labs holds first place in ARC-2 at 88.06, with Yi-Chia Chen’s Fields Model second at 87.22. In ARC-3 the order flips: Chen leads at 75.56 and Tufa is second at 70.02. Two teams sit at the top of both boards, and Cottaar has spent the week poking at Kaggle’s machinery out loud.

sections.heading: The experiment
sections.text:
In a forum thread asking whether things are back to normal, Cottaar said his team is “quite convinced” they are not. Every submission from his team, he reported, seems to lose about forty minutes: the model loads at normal speed once the notebook is running, but the notebook itself starts roughly forty minutes after the machine does.

How does he know? His team set a tripwire that stops a run if the machine has been up more than twenty minutes by the time the notebook begins. The tripwire kept firing, about forty minutes after each submission. And the lost time counts against the clock: the team’s successful runs last nine hours, not nine hours and forty minutes.

sections.heading: The control group
sections.text:
A day later he ran the cleaner test. A completely empty notebook, nothing attached, shows the same delay. It shows up with Kaggle’s June software setup and with its latest, and whether he submits from the United States or from Europe.

Submit an empty notebook with only the contest data attached on an RTX 6000 graphics card, he wrote, and it used to come back with an error within minutes. Now it takes fifty, while real submissions still run nine hours. His reading: notebooks take about fifty minutes to kick off, and the time is charged to the nine-hour budget. He names the rival explanation himself: the error may simply be returned late while true scores are not.

sections.heading: Enter CPMP
sections.text:
Into the thread walks the best-known name in the other camp. CPMP replied that a delay before a notebook runs “is not uncommon” and is not an issue, and asked whether Cottaar was discussing something else. Cottaar’s answer was the empty-notebook test.

No insults, no villains: two of the most decorated competitors in the field, politely at odds over a diagnosis, each with a stopwatch. Yi-Chia Chen, first on ARC-3, said the scores have been fluctuating and the cause could be infrastructure or plain variance; there is no telling which. The jury is the private board.

sections.heading: Everybody’s workaround
sections.text: The field has not waited for a verdict. xz, whose team faster machine is all you need is third on ARC-3, starts the games at the ten-minute mark whether or not the model server is up and sends a reset every seven minutes. Van-Phuc Huynh trades solving time for longer waiting and more resets to avoid a zero. Grigoriy Zatravkin, ninth on ARC-3, wondered whether probe runs like Tufa’s could leak information about the hidden games; xz replied that probes cost real submissions.

dispatches.headline: “A circus”: CPMP takes on Kaggle’s final weekend from third place on the ARC-2 board

image.alt: CPMP and Darragh’s opaque blue-and-gold starry avatar stand in an NVIDIA-themed hall filled with medals.
image.caption: CPMP and Darragh Hanley in the NV Banana hall, with Darragh’s starry Kaggle avatar.

sections.heading: One word from the top: circus
sections.text:
Friday night we told the world there would be no extension: the ARC Prize deadline stands at 11:59 pm UTC on Monday, queues or no queues. Saturday morning Jean-François Puget, CPMP, quoted our bulletin and put his own headline over the weekend. The ARC competitions on Kaggle, he wrote, have “turned into a circus”: most teams can’t submit in ARC-3, scoring takes more than a day in ARC-2, and the teams that do get a run see big swings in running speed and score. His verdict: “I never saw Kaggle platform being so bad since I started kaggling.”

Weigh the source. This is a man with a machine-learning PhD from, as he puts it, “a previous millennium,” who entered his first Kaggle contest in 2016, holds 29 competition golds and sits third on the ARC-2 board with Darragh Hanley. When he calls the building a circus, the building notices.

sections.heading: The theory of the case
sections.text:
CPMP does not just complain; he diagnoses. His case, from his own replies on Saturday: Kaggle launched its new Gemma competition on the same L4 graphics-card pool before ARC-AGI-2 had ended, and the trouble started at once. ARC-3’s crisis, he says, is storage, swamped by the very large number of Flash Next variants people are running. Replying to our own account, he called the Gemma contest on the same L4 pool a simpler explanation than agents: if agents were the problem, every competition would be hit.

Jack Cole of MindsAI guessed that Kaggle simply doesn’t have the GPUs. CPMP raised him: nor the storage, nor a uniform fleet of machines. And will the swings reorder the leaderboard? “We’ll know after deadline,” he wrote, once people report the gap between the public and private boards.

Those are CPMP’s diagnoses. Kaggle has not signed any of them.

sections.heading: Kaggle’s side of the ring
sections.text:
Kaggle’s people are not hiding; they are stretched. Walter Reade, whose X bio reads “AI at Google/Kaggle,” said in the same thread that resource use across Kaggle has jumped two to three times since the ARC competitions launched, with agents lowering the barrier to entry and contests growing more complicated.

On the forum, Kaggle staffer María Cruz told ARC-3 players the team is working on the broader platform issues but cannot look into individual submissions right now “due to capacity constraints.” On ARC-2 she said there will be no change to the deadline or the submission process in the final days. That reply sits at minus eighteen votes.

When CPMP reported that his team’s model-mount errors were hitting about two saves in three, he saved the notebook six times, every failure a mount failure, and submitted anyway hoping for a one-in-three shot. “We can’t work that way,” he wrote, and asked for his submission back. The one-in-three shot did not come in. Kaggle staffer Dustin answered that leftover poisoned cache entries in one region had been cleared and that a job was defragmenting the cache.

sections.heading: Who’s angry, and how
sections.text:
CPMP is far from alone, and the anger comes in flavors. His NVARC3 teammate Ivan Sorokin, posting as ivan, asked why Kaggle doesn’t just freeze the platform and disable submissions instead of fixing it quietly. Son Pham, whose Team Turducken is fourth on the ARC-3 board and is the head editor’s own entry, took a 0.00 with a gold medal in range and suggested reruns for the zeros or a freeze.

Over in ARC-2, Chan Kha Vu of V | A | M, ninth on the board, pointed out that with queues past twelve hours and scoring past twenty-four, a submission on the last day cannot finish in time. Chan is asking not for more submissions but for more time to pick a final one, and CPMP backed a fixed selection window after the close.

Not everyone is in the same corner. One competitor argued that rerunning only the zeros would be unfair, because every run lost time. And Yi-Chia Chen, first on ARC-3, says the scores have been swinging and the cause could be infrastructure or ordinary run-to-run variance; there is no telling which.

sections.heading: The banana in the middle
sections.text:
The loudest critic of the circus is also a contender in it. nvbanana, CPMP and Darragh Hanley, is third on the ARC-2 board at 83.89, behind Tufa Labs and Yi-Chia Chen. CPMP’s own advice to competitors is “evaluate your assumptions, evaluate your modifications,” and this weekend he has evaluated Kaggle’s. In 2025 he and Ivan Sorokin won ARC Prize as NVARC. Hanley, a Kaggle Grandmaster with 28 golds and a best-ever rank of fourth, is CPMP’s partner this year.

The private board decides on Monday night. Whatever it says, the banana had its say first.

dispatches.headline: Two crowns, two contests: Tufa leads ARC-2 by less than a point, Chen leads ARC-3 by five

image.alt: Two giant rabbits stand beside a towering fan-and-pipe citadel flying spider flags in a packed Colosseum, with a turkey-shaped war wagon, a cat, two terriers and four small figures on the sand below.
image.caption: Tufa’s citadel and Chen’s two rabbits, with the rest of the field on the sand below.

sections.heading: The same two names at the top of both boards
sections.text: Two days from the bell, the public leaderboards for ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3 have the same two teams in their top two places, in opposite order. In ARC-2, Tufa Labs leads at 88.06 and Yi-Chia Chen’s team, Fields Mode, is second at 87.22, less than a point behind. In ARC-3, Chen leads at 75.56 and Tufa is second at 70.02. ARC-2’s third place, nvbanana, is at 83.89, more than three points behind second. ARC-3’s third place, a team called faster machine is all you need, is at 58.59, more than eleven points behind Tufa.

sections.heading: How each crown was won
sections.text: Tufa’s ARC-2 score of 88.06 landed on October 9 and has not moved since, by our tracker’s reading of the public board. Chen closed on it through October, and on October 29 at 2:52 pm Eastern climbed from 84.72 to 87.22. ARC-3 went the other way. Tufa took the lead on October 13 at 68.91, and Chen passed on October 25 at 71.48, then reached 75.56 on October 27 at 2:14 am Eastern. Tufa answered with 70.02 on October 29, but has not matched it. Chen’s climb on that board began from 67.49 on October 22.

sections.heading: The 85 percent line
sections.text: On October 9, ARC Prize said a $150,000 bonus, on top of the guaranteed prizes, would be split among all teams scoring over 85 percent in ARC-2. Only two teams are above that line on the public board: Tufa and Chen. The next team, nvbanana at 83.89, is just over a point below it. Kaggle’s María Cruz said the 85 percent test is based on the private leaderboard, which becomes visible only after Kaggle finishes scoring the final submissions, so the public order is a guide, not a result.

sections.heading: Who they are
sections.text: ARC Prize named Tufa Labs and its Duck agent the first-place open-source solution for the June 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Milestone 1 prize. Tufa lists Dries Smit, Isaiah Pressman and Jeroen Cottaar among its AI researchers. Yi-Chia Chen is a Kaggle Competitions Master and a double-degree student at National Taiwan University and Waseda University. Chen’s public Kaggle account, threerabbits, shows an avatar of two rabbits. Chen also wrote a third-place solution write-up for Kaggle’s Eedi math-misconceptions contest.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.text: Both teams can still change their final picks until the bell at 11:59 pm UTC Monday, which is 6:59 pm Eastern. Kaggle lets each team choose up to two final submissions, and the private leaderboard decides. With ARC Prize telling competitors there will be no extension, the question is whether either team has a stronger run in the queue, in either contest, before Monday evening.

dispatches.editorNote: Overnight team update and picture commissioned by Mark Barney. Jack Cole’s historical record was checked against ARC Prize’s official results, newsletters and credited paper. Card images preserve their own printed dates.
dispatches.headline: The lab that wouldn’t sleep: ARC Mutants grind on, with an ARC legend in the chair

image.alt: The four ARC Mutants work overnight in a vaulted academy laboratory: Mark repairs a GPU rack, Jack guides floating colored grids from his command chair, Son works the submission console and violet-helmeted Ronen contains a runaway grid experiment. Error icons and stalled submission queues fill the monitors.
image.caption: ARC Mutants, still at the bench: Jack Cole, Mark Barney, Son Pham and Ronen.

sections.heading: One more experiment
sections.text: The ARC Mutants have not left the bench. Mark Barney, this paper’s editor and a member of the team, reports that the four are still grinding through grid experiments, last-minute submissions and Kaggle errors. This overnight mini-special comes from our own laboratory: Jack Cole, Mark, Son Pham and Ronen, still trying to make the next experiment count.

sections.heading: The experiment keeps escaping
sections.text: Our new scene catches the academy in full midnight disorder. Mark is elbow-deep in the GPU rack; Jack directs the colored grids from his command chair; Son works the submission console; Ronen catches the runaway puzzle in a violet grid shield. The monitors have their own contribution: queued, error, retry. The professor at the center of that tableau has earned more than a costume.

sections.heading: Jack Cole: the legend at the bench
sections.text: Jack Cole is not a cameo in this laboratory. In July 2024, ARC Prize credited Cole, Michael Hodel and Mohamed Osman’s MindsAI with the first score above the forty-percent barrier. A month later the organizers were congratulating Cole and MindsAI on a third consecutive world record. MindsAI finished the 2024 competition with the highest private-evaluation score in the field. The distinction matters: it was the top-scoring entry, while the official high-score prize went to the ARChitects because MindsAI did not open-source its solution.

sections.heading: The score and the paper
sections.text: The following year brought an official third-place finish for MindsAI and recognition on the paper track. ARC Prize awarded an honorable mention to Cole and Mohamed Osman’s “Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater: How and why deep learning for ARC.” The paper makes their case for deep learning that keeps learning at test time. A podium, a published argument and a method to explain: that is a serious ARC back catalogue.

sections.heading: Across the generations of ARC
sections.text: His record reaches into the interactive games, too. ARC Prize lists Cole as adviser and reviewer for StochasticGoose at Tufa Labs, winner of the 2025 ARC-AGI-3 Preview agent competition, with Dries Smit as lead developer. Now the archive’s circuit-board headset belongs beside Mark, Son and Ronen in the ARC Mutants laboratory. The Professor X character is an affectionate picture; the competitive history behind it is real.
